description: Comprehensive training on ladder selection, inspection, setup, safe use, and fall prevention.

slides.title: Welcome to Ladder Safety Training
slides.text: This course teaches employees how to safely select, inspect, set up, climb, and work from ladders in the workplace. Ladder accidents continue to cause serious injuries and lost work time in construction, maintenance, warehousing, and general industry. Most of these incidents can be prevented when workers understand the hazards and follow safe procedures every time they use a ladder.

slides.title: Why Ladder Safety Matters
slides.text: Falls from ladders can lead to broken bones, head injuries, spinal injuries, and even death. Many ladder incidents happen because workers rush, use the wrong ladder, or fail to inspect the equipment before climbing. Ladder safety matters because a simple mistake made at only a few feet off the ground can have life-changing consequences.

slides.title: Important Safety Principle
slides.text: Using the correct ladder correctly is one of the most important ways to prevent workplace falls and serious injuries.

slides.title: Common Ladder Types
slides.text: Workers may use step ladders, extension ladders, platform ladders, fixed ladders, and specialty ladders depending on the task. Each ladder type is designed for a specific purpose and should only be used as intended by the manufacturer. Choosing the wrong ladder type can create instability, reduce access, and increase the chance of a fall.

slides.title: Step Ladders
slides.text: Step ladders are self-supporting ladders commonly used for lower-height tasks. They should always be fully opened with the spreaders locked into place before use. Step ladders must never be leaned against a wall like an extension ladder because they are not designed for that purpose.

slides.title: Extension Ladders
slides.text: Extension ladders are used to reach higher areas and must be placed against a stable support surface. These ladders require proper angle, stable footing, and secure upper contact points to be used safely. If an extension ladder is set too steep or too shallow, it can slip or tip during use.

slides.title: Choosing the Right Ladder
slides.text: The right ladder must match the height of the work, the environment, and the weight it must support. Workers should consider their body weight, clothing, tools, and materials when selecting a ladder. A ladder that is too short encourages unsafe climbing, while an underrated ladder can fail under load.

slides.title: Ladder Selection Guidelines
steps: Choose a ladder that is tall enough for the job without standing on prohibited rungs.
Check the ladder duty rating to ensure it supports the worker and equipment.
Use fiberglass ladders near electrical hazards instead of metal ladders.
Select the correct ladder type for the work area and task.

slides.question: What should you consider when selecting a ladder?
options: Only the color of the ladder
Height, duty rating, and work environment
Only how light it is to carry
slides.correctText: Correct. A ladder should be chosen based on height, duty rating, and the job conditions.
slides.incorrectText: Incorrect. The best ladder choice depends on the work height, load, and environment.

slides.question: A step ladder can be used safely when leaned against a wall if someone holds it.
slides.correctText: Correct. Step ladders are self-supporting and should not be leaned against a wall.
slides.incorrectText: Incorrect. Step ladders are not designed to be used in a leaned position.

slides.title: Inspect Before Every Use
slides.text: Every ladder should be inspected before each use, even if it was used earlier in the day. Damage can happen during transport, storage, or previous work activities. A quick inspection helps identify defects before they lead to a failure while someone is climbing or working.

slides.title: What to Look for During Inspection
slides.text: Inspect the side rails, rungs, steps, locking devices, spreaders, feet, and labels. Look for cracks, bends, loose parts, corrosion, missing hardware, or worn feet that could reduce stability. If any structural part is damaged or questionable, the ladder should be taken out of service immediately.

slides.title: Out of Service
slides.text: Never use a ladder that is damaged, bent, missing parts, or otherwise unsafe. Tag it and remove it from service.

slides.title: Basic Inspection Procedure
steps: Check rails and steps for visible damage or defects.
Test locks, spreaders, and moving parts for proper operation.
Inspect ladder feet for traction and wear.
Confirm labels and safety markings are present and readable.

slides.question: When should a ladder be inspected?
slides.correctText: Correct. Ladders should be inspected before every use.
slides.incorrectText: Incorrect. A ladder should be checked each time before it is used.

slides.question: A ladder with a loose rung can still be used for a quick job.
slides.correctText: Correct. Any structural defect makes the ladder unsafe to use.
slides.incorrectText: Incorrect. A loose rung is a serious hazard and the ladder must be removed from service.

slides.title: Proper Ladder Setup
slides.text: Ladders must be placed on firm, level, and stable surfaces before use. Soft soil, gravel, slippery floors, clutter, and uneven ground can all reduce ladder stability. Proper setup is one of the most important steps in preventing movement, tipping, and sudden loss of balance.

slides.title: The 4-to-1 Rule
slides.text: When setting up an extension ladder, use the 4-to-1 rule to achieve the proper climbing angle. For every 4 feet of working ladder height, the base should be placed 1 foot away from the structure. This angle helps prevent the ladder from slipping outward or tipping backward.

points.text: Place feet on a solid, level surface.
Extend above the landing area when required.

slides.title: Securing the Ladder
slides.text: Whenever possible, ladders should be secured at the top, bottom, or both to prevent shifting. In high-traffic areas, the work zone should be protected so no one bumps the ladder during use. A ladder that moves unexpectedly can cause a worker to lose balance instantly.

slides.question: What is the correct setup ratio for an extension ladder?
slides.correctText: Correct. The safe setup guideline is the 4-to-1 rule.
slides.incorrectText: Incorrect. Extension ladders should generally be set using the 4-to-1 rule.

slides.question: It is acceptable to place a ladder on an uneven surface if the worker is experienced.
slides.correctText: Correct. Uneven surfaces make ladders unstable and unsafe.
slides.incorrectText: Incorrect. Experience does not make an unstable ladder safe.

slides.title: Safe Climbing Practices
slides.text: Always face the ladder when climbing up or down and keep your movements slow and controlled. Grasp the side rails or other approved climbing surfaces with your hands. Safe climbing requires attention, balance, and a steady pace from the moment you step onto the ladder until you step off.

slides.title: Three Points of Contact
slides.text: Three points of contact means keeping either two hands and one foot, or two feet and one hand, in contact with the ladder at all times. This improves stability and reduces the chance of slipping. Letting go with both hands or climbing while carrying items in your hands greatly increases the risk of a fall.

slides.title: Safe Climbing Procedure
steps: Face the ladder while climbing or descending.
Maintain three points of contact whenever possible.
Keep your body centered between the rails.
Carry tools in a belt or hoist them separately.

slides.question: How many points of contact should be maintained while climbing a ladder?
slides.correctText: Correct. Three points of contact helps maintain balance and control.
slides.incorrectText: Incorrect. The standard safe climbing practice is to maintain three points of contact.

slides.question: A worker should face away from the ladder when climbing down so they can see the floor.
slides.correctText: Correct. Workers should face the ladder when climbing up or down.
slides.incorrectText: Incorrect. Facing the ladder is the safe climbing method.

slides.title: Avoid Overreaching
slides.text: Overreaching happens when a worker leans too far to one side instead of repositioning the ladder. This shifts the body's center of gravity outside the rails and can cause the ladder to tip. A good rule is to keep your belt buckle or torso centered between the ladder side rails at all times.

slides.title: Electrical Hazards
slides.text: Metal ladders conduct electricity and can become deadly if they contact energized equipment or overhead power lines. Workers should always look up and around before raising or moving a ladder. Fiberglass ladders are the preferred choice when electrical exposure is possible because they are nonconductive under normal use conditions.

slides.title: Weather and Surface Conditions
slides.text: Rain, snow, ice, mud, oil, and high wind can all make ladder work more dangerous. Slippery footwear and contaminated rungs reduce traction and increase the chance of slipping. Before using a ladder, evaluate the environment and decide whether conditions make the task unsafe.

slides.question: What should you do if you cannot comfortably reach your work area?
options: Have a coworker pull the ladder toward the work
slides.correctText: Correct. The ladder should be repositioned so the worker stays centered.
slides.incorrectText: Incorrect. Repositioning the ladder is the safest choice.

slides.question: Fiberglass ladders are a better choice when working near electrical hazards.
slides.correctText: Correct. Fiberglass ladders are preferred near electricity.
slides.incorrectText: Incorrect. Fiberglass ladders are the safer option near electrical hazards.

slides.title: Working From a Ladder
slides.text: When working from a ladder, both feet should remain secure on the ladder and the worker should avoid sudden or jerking movements. Tools and materials should be managed so the worker can maintain balance and avoid dropping objects. If the task requires excessive force, long reach, or heavy material handling, a ladder may not be the right equipment for the job.

slides.title: Top Rung Warning
slides.text: Never stand on the top rung, top step, or top cap of a ladder unless the ladder is specifically designed and labeled for that purpose.

slides.title: Common Causes of Ladder Falls
slides.text: Ladder falls commonly result from poor inspection, unstable setup, using the wrong ladder, overreaching, climbing with items in the hands, and standing on prohibited steps. Many accidents are linked to shortcuts and rushing. Workers who slow down and follow safe procedures are far less likely to be injured.

slides.title: Review Checkpoint
slides.text: You have now covered ladder selection, inspection, setup, climbing, and major hazards. The next slides review the most important safety points.

slides.question: Which of the following is a common cause of ladder falls?
slides.correctText: Correct. Overreaching is a major cause of ladder instability and falls.
slides.incorrectText: Incorrect. Overreaching is one of the most common ladder hazards.

slides.question: What should be done with a damaged ladder?
options: Use it only for quick jobs
Tag it and remove it from service
slides.correctText: Correct. Unsafe ladders must be removed from service immediately.
slides.incorrectText: Incorrect. A damaged ladder should be tagged and removed from service.

slides.question: Maintaining three points of contact improves stability while climbing.
slides.correctText: Correct. Three points of contact is a basic ladder safety practice.
slides.incorrectText: Incorrect. Three points of contact helps reduce slips and falls.

slides.question: What is the safest surface for ladder placement?
slides.correctText: Correct. Ladders should be placed on firm, level, stable surfaces.
slides.incorrectText: Incorrect. The safest ladder placement is on firm, level ground.

slides.title: Final Safety Reminder
slides.text: Safe ladder use depends on proper selection, inspection, setup, climbing technique, and constant attention to hazards. Every use matters.

questions.question: What is the 4-to-1 ladder rule?
options: 1 foot out for every 4 feet up
4 feet out for every 1 foot up
1 foot out for every 1 foot up

questions.question: You can stand on the top rung of a ladder.
What should a ladder be placed on?
Metal ladders are safe near electrical hazards.

slides.title: Course Complete
slides.text: Congratulations. You have completed the Ladder Safety Training course. You should now understand the key practices needed to reduce ladder hazards and work more safely.
